title: Can we tile a five by three grid with a corner removed?
description: A grid of five rows and three columns has its top right square removed. Fourteen squares are left, so seven tiles are needed. One lying tile covers the short top row, and upright tiles fill the rows below. Keeko's doubt, that a missing square spoils it, is struck.
teaching_notes: One idea: cover the short row first, then fill the full rows with upright tiles. Watch for students who think a missing square makes tiling impossible.

source: A 5 × 3 grid (5 rows, 3 columns) has its top right square re
video_script.why: The child sees that a grid with a square removed can still be tiled when the squares left can be covered row by row.
video_script.substitution: The two squares left in the top row take one lying tile, and each full pair of rows takes three upright tiles.
video_script.anchor: A grid of unit squares with 5 rows and 3 columns, its top right square removed, and a tile that covers 2 squares.
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko thinks a missing square spoils it. But the hole is not part of the region, so we cover only the squares that are left.
video_script.payoff_line: Yes, one horizontal tile in the top row and six vertical tiles below cover the grid.

final_answer.value: Yes: 1 horizontal tile in the top row and 6 vertical tiles below
final_answer.spoken: yes, one horizontal tile in the top row and six vertical tiles below

hold_back: 1 horizontal tile in the top row and 6 vertical tiles below
maths_rules: The grid has 5 × 3 = 15 squares, and 1 is removed, so 14 are left.
Top row: the two squares left form one horizontal tile.
Rows 2 and 3: a vertical tile in each of the 3 columns, 3 tiles.
Rows 4 and 5: a vertical tile in each of the 3 columns, 3 tiles.
1 + 3 + 3 = 7 tiles, with no gaps and no overlaps.
Slip: a missing square does not spoil a tiling; cover only the squares that are left.
video_script.design: One grid with a corner square removed. The short top row is covered first, then the full rows below. The slip is thinking a hole always spoils the tiling.
